one_liner: C++20 Ethereum Virtual Machine interpreter behind the EVMC API; about 3.5x faster than go-ethereum's EVM in evm-bench.
what_it_does: evmone executes EVM smart-contract bytecode as a standalone execution module: a client hands it code, a message and an EVMC host interface (state, storage, logs, nested calls) and gets back the result and gas left. It ships as a shared or static library exposing evmc_create_evmone(), plus test tools (state and blockchain fixtures, t8n) and precompiles up to the current Osaka/Amsterdam revisions. It is not a node or state database; the caller must supply the host, so using it inside geth needs an EVMC-enabled geth build (the README points to the Ewasm fork's releases).
how_it_is_fast: The default Baseline interpreter does only a minimal JUMPDEST analysis and dispatches with computed goto (switch dispatch on MSVC or with cgoto=no); it reuses per-call-depth execution states and does 256-bit arithmetic with the intx library and Keccak with ethash. The optional Advanced interpreter uses indirect call threading over a pre-analysed instruction table and charges gas and stack checks once per basic block, but its analysis is expensive; since 0.9.0 the Baseline is 18% faster than Advanced on the project's own suite. Linux and Windows x86-64 builds default to -march=x86-64-v2.
when_to_use: Building an Ethereum client, simulator, test harness or fuzzer in C/C++ that needs a fast, spec-tracking EVM behind a stable C ABI (EVMC).
Compute-heavy contract execution: in evm-bench evmone was the fastest of seven EVMs, 3.8x faster than geth on snailtracer and 1.3x faster than revm on the summed suite.
Running Ethereum execution-spec state or blockchain test fixtures quickly (the `evmone test` command recognises both formats).
Embedding EVM execution in non-Go stacks where linking geth is not an option (any language with a C FFI can load the EVMC module).
when_not_to_use: As a drop-in speedup for stock go-ethereum: upstream geth does not load EVMC modules, and in a real node the state database and host calls, which the benchmark mocked away on the evmone side, take a large share of block-processing time.

Consensus-critical deployments without your own differential testing: open issues include EIP-7702 consensus bugs (#1447, #1448, #1449, #1728) and a state-root divergence versus geth/revm (#1727, RIPEMD160 empty-account touch).

Precompile-heavy workloads with a default build: the README says ecrecover is implemented directly 'with degraded performance' (a libsecp256k1 option exists since 0.19.0) and expmod uses stubs unless EVMONE_PRECOMPILES_GMP=1 is set.
MSVC builds where interpreter speed matters: computed goto is not supported there, so the Baseline falls back to switch dispatch.
Old toolchains: C++20 and CMake 3.25 or newer are required.

integration.form: shared lib (EVMC module, BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults ON) | static lib
integration.dependencies: EVMC, intx, ethash (Keccak); optional GMP for full expmod, optional libsecp256k1 for ecrecover, blst for BLS precompiles; google/benchmark and googletest only for tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++20, CMake 3.25; changelog lists GCC 11, Clang 13, Visual Studio 2022 as minimum tested compilers and Xcode 16.2 for macOS
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux/Windows (x86-64-v2 by default, configurable via EVMONE_X86_64_ARCH_LEVEL), macOS, aarch64 Linux
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; lib/evmone/vm.hpp shows each VM instance reuses a per-call-depth ExecutionState vector and tracer chain without locking, so use one VM instance per thread.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: geth can use it only through an EVMC-enabled geth build (--vm.evm=./libevmone.so); otherwise it is a library with a different (EVMC) interface

gotchas: Harness flaw: evm-bench rounds every run to a whole millisecond before averaging (src/run.rs parses each runner line and stores Duration::from_millis(value.round())), so rows of a few milliseconds are coarse: ten-thousand-hashes at 2.4 ms and erc20.mint at 5 ms carry up to 0.5 ms quantisation per run, about 20% of the evmone figure, which makes their 5.5x and 3.4x ratios rough.

snailtracer, the row the record treats as the fair compute-bound comparison, runs only once per runner (num-runs 1, no warm-up) and is not pure compute: traceray copies every sphere (11 storage slots) and triangle (19 slots) from storage into memory for each ray and rand() writes the seed to storage, so its 3.8x also reflects geth's StateDB storage path versus evmc::MockedHost's unordered_map.

Host asymmetry: the evmone runner builds a fresh evmc::MockedHost per run, while geth runs through its full StateDB with access-list preparation and snapshot/revert; both runners use London rules (EVMC 10.0.0's EVMC_LATEST_STABLE_REVISION is EVMC_LONDON), so the fork rules match. Outputs are not cross-checked beyond a success status.

The table is from 2022 releases (evmone 0.9.1, go-ethereum v1.10.25) with no CPU or compiler stated; evmone has since released up to 0.24.0 (2026-09-23) and geth has had its own interpreter optimisations, so the current ratio is unmeasured here.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No EVM interpreter is catalogued yet; the siblings (Fizzy, wasm3, Wasmi, WAMR and others) execute WebAssembly, not EVM bytecode, so pick evmone whenever the input is EVM bytecode and one of those when it is Wasm. Outside the catalogue, revm (Rust) is the nearest alternative and was 1.3x slower than evmone in the same evm-bench table.
verified_claims_summary: The third-party evm-bench README times only the contract call (deployment excluded), averaging 5 runs (1 for snailtracer) each rounded to a whole millisecond: evmone 0.9.1 (CMake Release, compiler unnamed, on evmc::MockedHost) sums 66 ms versus 235 ms for go-ethereum v1.10.25's interpreter (go run, in-memory StateDB), with snailtracer 43 ms vs 163 ms; hardware is not stated.
status_note: Actively maintained by Pawel Bylica (Ipsilon), with releases tracking every Ethereum fork up to Amsterdam (0.24.0 on 2026-09-23) and commits on 2026-10-06; Apache-2.0 and copyable as a library, but consensus-critical users should watch the open EIP-7702 issues.
